format.description: Chọn hai nhóm khách mà buổi triển lãm của trường đại học hướng đến.
Chọn hai lý do khiến nhóm sinh viên quyết định giới thiệu Charles Dickens.
Ghép sáu tác phẩm của Dickens với chủ đề thảo luận được chọn.

explanations.21: Nhóm hướng tới người dân trong thành phố: sự kiện sẽ được quảng bá tại địa phương.
explanations.22: Nhóm hướng tới những người đang cân nhắc đăng ký học tại trường vào năm sau.
explanations.23: Cathy cho biết nhiều người biết Dickens, đã đọc tiểu thuyết hoặc xem phim chuyển thể.
explanations.24: Graham nhấn mạnh các tiểu thuyết phơi bày điều kiện sống tồi tệ và thúc đẩy thay đổi xã hội.
explanations.25: Nhóm đề xuất tập trung vào khía cạnh y tế/chăm sóc sức khỏe được nhắc tới trong tác phẩm.
explanations.26: Oliver Twist được gắn với chủ đề giáo dục.
explanations.27: Nicholas Nickleby được liên hệ với hoạt động giải trí.
explanations.28: Martin Chuzzlewit được sử dụng để đề cập đến những chuyến đi.
explanations.29: Nhóm tập trung vào câu chuyện cuộc đời nhân vật nữ trong Bleak House.
explanations.30: Nhóm muốn đề cập sự thay đổi địa vị tài chính, gắn với chủ đề của cải.

transcript.speaker: CATHY
transcript.text: OK, Graham, so let’s check we both know what we’re supposed to be doing.

transcript.speaker: GRAHAM
transcript.text: OK.

transcript.speaker: CATHY
transcript.text: So, for the university’s open day, we have to plan a display on British life and literature in the mid-19th century.

transcript.speaker: GRAHAM
transcript.text: That’s right. But we’ll have some people to help us find the materials and set it up, remember – for the moment, we just need to plan it.

transcript.speaker: CATHY
transcript.text: Good. So have you gathered who’s expected to come and see the display? Is it for the people studying English, or students from other departments? I’m not clear about it.

transcript.speaker: GRAHAM
transcript.text: Nor me. That was how it used to be, but it didn’t attract many people, so this year it’s going to be part of an open day, to raise the university’s profile. It’ll be publicised in the city, to encourage people to come and find out something of what does on here (Q21/Q22). And it’s included in the information that’s sent to people who are considering applying to study here next year. (Q21/Q22)

transcript.speaker: CATHY
transcript.text: Presumably some current students and lecturers will come?

transcript.speaker: GRAHAM
transcript.text: I would imagine so, but we’ve been told to concentrate on the other categories of people.

transcript.speaker: CATHY
transcript.text: Right. We don’t have to cover the whole range of 19th-century literature, do we?

transcript.speaker: GRAHAM
transcript.text: No, it’s entirely up to us. I suggest just using Charles Dickens.

transcript.speaker: CATHY
transcript.text: That’s a good idea. Most people have heard of him, and have probably read some of his novels, or seen films based on them (Q23/Q24), so that’s a good lead-in to life in his time.

transcript.speaker: GRAHAM
transcript.text: Exactly. And his novels show the awful conditions that most people had to live in, don’t they: he wanted to shock people into doing something about it. (Q23/Q24)

transcript.speaker: CATHY
transcript.text: Did he do any campaigning, other than writing?

transcript.speaker: GRAHAM
transcript.text: Yes, he campaigned for education and other social reforms, and gave talks, but I’m inclined to ignore that and focus on the novels.

transcript.speaker: CATHY
transcript.text: Yes, I agree.

transcript.speaker: CATHY
transcript.text: OK, so now shall we think about a topic linked to each novel?

transcript.speaker: GRAHAM
transcript.text: Yes. I’ve printed out a list of Dicken’s novels in the order they were published, in the hope you’d agree to focus on him!

transcript.speaker: CATHY
transcript.text: You’re lucky I did agree! Let’s have a look. OK, the first was The Pickwick Papers, published in 1836. It was very successful when it came out, wasn’t it, and was adapted for the theatre straight away.

transcript.speaker: GRAHAM
transcript.text: There’s an interesting point, though, that there’s a character who keeps falling asleep, and that medical condition was named after the book – Pickwickian Syndrome. (Q25)

transcript.speaker: CATHY
transcript.text: Oh, so why don’t we use that as the topic, and include some quotations from the novel?

transcript.speaker: GRAHAM
transcript.text: Right, Next is Oliver Twist. There’s a lot in the novel about poverty. But maybe something less obvious …

transcript.speaker: CATHY
transcript.text: Well Oliver is taught how to steal, isn’t he? We could use that to illustrate the fact that very few children went to school, particularly not poor children, so they learnt in other ways. (Q26)

transcript.speaker: GRAHAM
transcript.text: Good idea. What’s next?

transcript.speaker: CATHY
transcript.text: Maybe Nicholas Nickleby. Actually he taught in a really cruel school, didn’t he?

transcript.speaker: GRAHAM
transcript.text: That’s right. But there’s also the company of touring actors that Nicholas joins. We could do something on theatres and other amusements of the time. (Q27) We don’t want only the bad things, do we?

transcript.speaker: CATHY
transcript.text: OK.

transcript.speaker: GRAHAM
transcript.text: What about Martin Chuzzlewit? He goes to the USA, doesn’t he?

transcript.speaker: CATHY
transcript.text: Yes, and Dickens himself had been there a year before, and drew on his experience there in the novel. (Q28)

transcript.speaker: GRAHAM
transcript.text: I wonder, though … The main theme is selfishness, so we could do something on social justice? No, too general, let’s keep to your idea – I think it would work well.

transcript.speaker: CATHY
transcript.text: He wrote Bleak House next – that’s my favourite of his novels.

transcript.speaker: GRAHAM
transcript.text: Yes, mine too. His satire of the legal system is pretty powerful.

transcript.speaker: CATHY
transcript.text: That’s true, but think about Esther, the heroine. As a child she lives with someone she doesn’t know is her aunt, who treats her very badly. Then she’s very happy living with her guardian, and he puts her in charge of the household. And at the end she gets married and her guardian gives her and her husband a house, where of course they’re very happy. (Q29)

transcript.speaker: GRAHAM
transcript.text: Yes, I like that.

transcript.speaker: CATHY
transcript.text: What shall we take next? Little Dorrit? Old Mr Dorrit has been in a debtors’ prison for years …

transcript.speaker: GRAHAM
transcript.text: So was Dicken’s father, wasn’t he?

transcript.speaker: CATHY
transcript.text: That’s right.

transcript.speaker: GRAHAM
transcript.text: What about focusing on the part when Mr Dorrit inherits a fortune, and he starts pretending he’s always been rich? (Q30)

transcript.speaker: CATHY
transcript.text: Good idea.

transcript.speaker: GRAHAM
transcript.text: OK, so next we need to think about what materials we want to illustrate each issue. That’s going to be quite hard.

pairQuestions.question: Which TWO groups of people are the display organisers particularly encouraged to attract?
choices: Students already studying at the university
People thinking about applying to the university

pairQuestions.question: Which TWO reasons do Cathy and Graham give for choosing Charles Dickens?
choices: His public campaigns are the central theme of the display
Many people already know his stories through books or films
His novels draw attention to difficult social conditions
They intend to cover every nineteenth-century author
His speeches are better known than his novels
